title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream deterministic validation and at‑most‑one permitted repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired discordants n10=5 (guarded only), n01=0 (baseline only). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (>0.05), so the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive summary only. Five validator‑triggered repairs consumed five extra model calls; total model calls = 1005. We interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in the context of extremely high baseline validity, sparse discordant counts, the shared_initial_candidate design that isolates downstream effects, and deterministic validator scope.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations can reduce manual effort but introduces safety risks: misordered operations, transient invariant violations, and modifications to protected interfaces that can disrupt service. Prior empirical and survey literature documents hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures for code‑like generation tasks and motivates architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This study asks a tightly specified question under a frozen preregistration: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), to what degree can a deterministic downstream validator plus at most one allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes relative to reusing the identical initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The paired design deliberately isolates downstream interventions (validation and an at‑most‑one repair) so any observed paired difference must arise from those downstream mechanisms rather than from independent first‑pass sampling, prompt engineering, or decoding constraints. That isolation positions the study to quantify the marginal benefit of validator‑driven repair under controlled assumptions about generator behavior and validator coverage.
sections.related_work:
Empirical studies and surveys show frequent LLM errors on structured generation tasks and motivate verifier‑augmented pipelines to reduce harmful or non‑executable outputs [3],[4]. Work on constrained or schema‑aware decoding demonstrates reductions in syntactic and executability errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations originate outside NetOps and thus rely on validator fidelity when ported to network workflows [5],[6]. Recent NetOps/system proposals emphasize guarded architectures, canary/rollback stages, and governance/proof‑carrying designs to mitigate automation risks; these contributions provide architectures, prototypes, and benchmarks that illustrate how validator coverage and orchestration policies determine operational reliability more than any single model alone [7],[8],[9].

Our experiment complements this literature by preregistering a paired comparison whose estimand isolates the incremental effect of downstream deterministic validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant. This avoids conflating downstream intervention effects with differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting strategies and so clarifies what a validator+repair layer can contribute in isolation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design fidelity. The full preregistration (study id cand‑003‑stud‑001) fixed a paired binary confirmatory design with task_count = 1000 and generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. The guarded pipeline could deterministically reject the shared candidate and invoke at most one permitted repair call; no independent first‑pass generations for the two conditions were performed. The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rates (guarded minus baseline) and the preregistered confirmatory test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729).

Model and validator configuration. The declared provider/model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The recorded model configuration shows temperature = null/unset; null/unset is explicitly not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The runtime adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). The validator implements deterministic emulation‑based checks for required command presence and ordering, protected‑interface noninterference, and workflow invariants; it emits a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict and structured traces used for scoring and repair triggers.

Task corpus and executor contracts. Tasks were drawn deterministically from the preregistered challenging_workflow_stress_v1 profile, producing 1000 unique paired intents intended to exercise ordering and multi‑device invariants (difficulty labels included very_hard and extreme in the task profile). The executor followed the preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion rules: maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, and complete_pair_primary missingness treatment. All seeds, selection rules, and executor code were fixed before any hosted‑model invocation and recorded in the archived manifest.

Analysis plan and interpretation of shared_initial_candidate semantics. The analysis executor implemented the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar for the paired contingency table and computed the preregistered paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as a descriptive summary. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, any paired improvement must result from deterministic validator decisions or from the permitted repair call; the design therefore provides a conservative estimate of the incremental contribution of validation+repair separate from generator‑level interventions.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. Execution completed as preregistered: planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call accounting records 1005 hosted model call events: 1000 shared initial generations and 5 repair invocations. No cross‑condition cache reuse or contamination flags were observed.

Primary paired contingency and preregistered inferential outcome. The observed paired table is n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Marginal observed rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The exact two‑sided McNemar test (preregistered primary confirmatory test) yields p = 0.0625, which does not meet two‑sided α = 0.05; therefore the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis is not supported.

Preregistered descriptive summaries and repair diagnostics. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive statistic only. The executor produced per‑task deterministic validator traces: the five validator‑triggered repairs were invoked when the shared initial candidate violated required_sequence constraints or touched protected interfaces; in each repaired episode the repair call produced a modified candidate that the validator then accepted. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). The small number of discordant pairs produces the discrete exact‑McNemar p‑value boundary (with n10=5, n01=0 the two‑sided p = 0.0625). An unregistered one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline) yields p = 0.03125 and is explicitly reported as exploratory/post‑hoc only.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive interpretation and power implications. The preregistered confirmatory result is the exact two‑sided McNemar p = 0.0625; by the preregistration this fails to reject at two‑sided α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) was a preregistered descriptive summary and excludes zero because bootstrap resampling with extremely sparse discordant counts can yield nonzero percentile bounds; that descriptive statistic does not overturn the preregistered confirmatory outcome. The preregistered power plan had assumed a baseline ≈ 0.60 and targeted an absolute increase of 0.15; the observed baseline (0.995) departs sharply from that assumption and produces very few discordant pairs, substantially reducing sensitivity to small absolute improvements under exact paired tests. Thus the nondetection at two‑sided α = 0.05 primarily reflects limited statistical power in the observed high‑accuracy regime rather than proving absence of any practical benefit in settings with higher baseline failure prevalence.

Mechanistic reading under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because baseline and guarded episodes began from the identical initial candidate, the five observed discordant pairs demonstrate only downstream validator and permitted repair effects. Validator traces indicate the five repairs addressed required_sequence violations or protected‑interface touches; in each case a single permitted repair call produced an accepted candidate. These traces show that validator coverage can correct particular ordering and protected‑field errors but also reveal where the validator did not trigger repairs (most shared candidates were already valid). Disentangling whether low repair incidence is caused by generator competence, corpus composition, or validator conservatism would require follow‑ups that vary generator sampling, repair budget, and validator rule sets; such variations were not part of the frozen preregistration and were therefore not executed here.

Failure‑mode and difficulty considerations. The preregistered task profile includes very_hard and extreme workflow patterns designed to exercise multi‑step ordering and multi‑interface invariants. Representative validator traces in the archive show repaired episodes arising from sequence misordering or protected‑interface touches; the archive also contains many accepted candidates whose normalized configurations matched required sequences. Because the executor enforced single initial‑generation reuse, these observations speak to the interaction between generator behavior for the chosen model+prompt and the validator rule coverage rather than to effects of alternative prompting or constrained decoding.

Operational implications and recommended preregistered follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence indicates that downstream validator‑guided repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic NetOps stress scenarios, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. To assess practical operational value we recommend preregistered follow‑ups that (a) include independent first‑pass generation arms or constrained‑decoding arms to measure generator‑level interventions, (b) sweep repair budgets (0..k repairs) with prespecified confirmatory contrasts, (c) expand validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity, and (d) include multiple model families and sampling parameter settings (recorded as nonnull parameters) so power calculations match plausible baseline failure rates. Each follow‑up should prespecify primary tests and multiplicity adjustments.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study (shared_initial_candidate semantics) on 1000 synthetic NetOps tasks, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline yielded a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls = 1005. The primary inferential outcome remains the preregistered exact McNemar result; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is explicitly labeled exploratory/post‑hoc. These archived, artifact‑grounded results show that downstream validator/repair safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes but that measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. The archived preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts support reproducibility and motivate preregistered follow‑ups that broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

Preregistration: study cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls and recorded in the archived execution manifest). limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
